During the {{c1::7th}} week of development , the obliteration of the vitelline duct (omphalomesenteric duct) occurs |||
If the vitelline duct COMPLETELY fails to close , a vitelline {{c1::fistula (persistent vitelline duct)}} develops, which is characterized by {{c2::meconium}} discharge from the umbilicus |||
If the vitelline duct only closes partially , a(n) {{c1::Meckel}} diverticulum develops, with the patent portion attached to the ileum |||

{{c1::Polyhydramnios}} is the presence of too much amniotic fluid and may be associated with fetal malformations such as anencephaly and esophageal or duodenal atresia (inability to swallow) ||| - Anencephaly and GI atresia lead to inability of fetus to swallow - Also associated with maternal diabet
A(n) {{c1:: patent urachus }} occurs due to total failure of the urachus to obliterate ||| AKA urachal fistula Photo credit: Ghattas et al. , CC BY 4.0 , via Frontiers

A patent {{c2:: urachus }} presents as straw-colored {{c1:: urine }} discharge from the umbilicus with {{c3:: erythema }} around the area ||| - This is exacerbated by crying, straining, or prone position - vs. a vitelline fistula which will result in a meconium discharge from the umbilicus
How do levels of AFP change in a fetus with open neural tube defects ? {{c1::Increased}} |||

The remnant of the umbilical vein is the {{c1:: ligamentum teres hepatis }}, which is contained in the {{c2:: falciform ligament }} |||
Lung development begins with development of a(n) {{c1::lung bud}} from the distal end of the respiratory diverticulum |||

The kidneys lie in the {{c1:: retroperitoneal }} cavity of the body |||

{{c1:: Syringomyelia }} is a dilated , fluid-filled , cystic cavity within the central canal of the spinal cord ||| - The widened bubble or cavitation first damages neural fibers passing near the center of the spine - Can be secondary to tumor / trauma (whiplash) or congenital (associated with Chiar

Syringomyelia most commonly occurs at spinal cord levels {{c1::C2}} - {{c1::T9}} ||| Photo credit: File:Syringomyelia.jpg: Cyborg Ninja at English Wikipedia (uploaded by User:ToNToNi Derivative work: User:SUM1 , CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

Syringomyelia results in damage to the {{c2:: spinothalamic }} tract 2nd-order neurons crossing in the {{c1::anterior white commissure}} ||| - Typically, there is cavitation of the cord in the cervical region - At the level of the lesion, there is bilateral loss of pain and temperature - The disease

{{c4:: Syringomyelia }} results in {{c3:: bi }} lateral loss of {{c1:: pain }} and {{c1:: temperature }} sensation in a(n) "{{c2:: cape-like }}" distribution ||| - Pain loss may present as cuts not felt - Temperature loss may present as burns not felt Photo credit: Internet Archive Book Images , (im

Syringomyelia typically results in pain/temperature deficits in the {{c1:: upper }} extremities ||| - Pain loss may present as cuts not felt - Temp loss may present as burns not felt - Most common locations Cervical > Thoracic >>> Lumbar (" cape-like " distribution) Photo credit: Internet Archive Bo

Syrinx expansion in syringomyelia may lead to damage to the {{c1::lower::lower/upper}} motor neurons of the anterior horn ||| - Causes muscle atrophy and weakness with decreased muscle tone and impaired reflexes - May also causes paresis of paravertebral muscles resulting in a scoliosis Photo credit

Syrinx expansion in syringomyelia (late stage) may cause {{c1::Horner}} syndrome ||| Due to disruption of the lateral horn Photo credit: Fion Bremner , CC BY 4.0 , via Frontiers in Neurology (above); Kikkeri et al. , CC BY 3.0 , via Cureus (below)

{{c2::Syringomyelia}} is a spinal cord lesion that arises with {{c1:: trauma }} and tumors or in association with {{c1:: Chiari I }} malformation ||| SYRING e has 1 needle Photo credit: Modified OpenStax , CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons Photo credit: File:Syringomyelia.jpg: Cyborg Ninja at Englis

Chiari {{c2::I}} malformation is characterized by downward displacement of the {{c1::cerebellar tonsils}} through the foramen magnum ||| Cerebellar tonsillar ectopia > 3 - 5 mm Photo credit: Hellerhoff , CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons
Chiari {{c1::I}} malformation is congenital and is mostly asymptomatic in childhood |||

Chiari I malformation may present as paroxysmal occipital {{c1::headaches}} and cerebellar symptoms ||| - Headaches are due to meningeal irritation, cerebellar dysfunction (e.g., ataxia) due to compression of cerebellar tonsils - Symptoms often worsen with the Valsalva maneuver
What disease is associated with this spinal cord lesion ? {{c1::Syringomyelia}} ||| Photo credit: Modified OpenStax , CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons
{{c1:: Neural tube }} defects arise due to failure of the neuropores to fuse by the {{c2::4th}} week of pregnancy ||| Leaves a persistent connection between the amniotic cavity and the spinal canal
{{c2:: Neural tube }} defects are associated with low {{c1:: folate }} levels prior to conception and during pregnancy ||| Folate = vitamin B 9

Open neural tube defects are detected during prenatal care by {{c2:: elevated }} {{c1:: alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)}} levels in the amniotic fluid and maternal blood ||| Spina bifida occulta presents with normal AFP levels because it is a closed neural tube defect rather than an open neural tube defect

Elevated {{c1:: acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) ::2}} in amniotic fluid are helpful confirmatory tests for suspected neural tube defects when ultrasound findings are inconclusive ||| - Initial screening test at 16-18 weeks looks for increased maternal serum AFP - Fetal AChE/A

{{c1::Anencephaly}} is the absence of the skull and brain , resulting in an open calvarium with an absent forebrain ||| Anencephaly is a failure of the anterior (rostral) neuropore to close Photo credit: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental D

What pathology is associated with disruption of the cranial end of the neural tube ? {{c1::Anencephaly}} ||| Photo credit: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
{{c2::Anencephaly}} leads to a(n) "{{c1:: frog-like }}" appearance of the fetus due to prominent eyes ||| Photo credit: Ed Uthman, MD , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Anencephaly is characterized by {{c1:: elevated }} levels of AFP in utero ||| Photo credit: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Anencephaly may result in {{c1:: poly }} hydramnios ||| Swallowing is impaired due to lack of a swallowing center in the brain Photo credit: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

{{c2:: Anencephaly }} and spina bifida are neural tube defects associated with folate deficiency and/or maternal {{c1:: diabetes }} ||| - A nencephaly caused by high A 1C - Risk factors are typically multifactorial which can include folate deficiency during pregnancy, drugs that interfere with folat

{{c1::Holoprosencephaly}} is due to failure of the forebrain to divide into 2 cerebral hemispheres ||| Example of malformation Photo credit: Pallangyo et al. , CC BY 4.0 , via Journal of Medical Case Reports, modified by removing arrows
The left and right hemispheres usually separate during weeks {{c1::3}} - {{c1::4}} of development ||| Photo credit: OpenStax , CC BY 4.0

Holoprosencephaly may be related to mutations in the {{c1::Sonic hedgehog}} signaling pathway ||| This is an example of a developmental field defect which is when an initial embryonic disturbance leads to multiple malformations by disrupting the development of adjacent tissues and structures within

The moderate form of holoprosencephaly presents with {{c1::cleft lip/palate}} ||| Photo credit: James Heilman, MD , CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons, modified by censoring Photo credit: CDC , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

The severe form of holoprosencephaly results in {{c1::cyclopia (one eye)}} and a primitive nasal structure (proboscis) ||| Midfacial clefts seen as well Photo credit: BC Hirst & GA Piersol , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Photo credit: Dingana et al. , CC BY 4.0 , via Clinical Medical Reviews

Holoprosencephaly is seen in {{c1:: Patau }} syndrome and {{c2:: fetal alcohol }} syndrome ||| - In Patau (trisomy 13), there is a defect in the fusion of the prechordal mesoderm , an integral embryonic structure affecting growth of the midface, eyes, and forebrain → catastrophic midline defects - F
Spina bifida is due to failure of the {{c1::posterior}} vertebral arch to close ||| Photo credit: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

What pathology is associated with disruption of the caudal end of the neural tube ? {{c1::Spina bifida}} ||| Photo credit: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Which form of spina bifida is associated with failure of the bony spinal canal to close but with no herniation ? {{c1::Spina bifida occulta}} ||| Photo credit: OpenStax , CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons
Spina bifida occulta is usually seen at {{c1::lower::upper or lower}} vertebral levels |||
Is the dura intact in spina bifida occulta ? {{c1::Yes}} |||

Which form of spina bifida is associated with a tuft of hair or skin dimple at the level of the bone defect? {{c1::Spina bifida occulta}} ||| Other potential cutaneous manifestations include hemangioma or nevus Photo credit: OpenStax , CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons
Spina bifida occulta is characterized by {{c1:: normal }} levels of AFP in utero ||| The exception to the rule of increased AFP with neural tube defects
Which form of spina bifida is associated with herniation of meninges (but no neural tissue) through the bony defect? {{c1::Meningocele}} ||| Photo credit: OpenStax , CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons
Which form of spina bifida is associated with herniation of meninges and neural tissue through the bony defect? {{c1::Myelomeningocele}} ||| Photo credit: OpenStax , CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

{{c2::Dandy-Walker}} malformation is caused by failure of the 4th ventricle to close, which leads to congenital hypoplasia of the {{c1::cerebellar vermis}} ||| - Disruption of HOX gene expression in rhombencephalon disrupts mesenchymal development in the metencephalon - This disrupts angiogenesis, c

Dandy-Walker malformation (DWM) is associated with {{c1:: non-communicating hydrocephalus }} and {{c2:: spina bifida }} ||| - Noncommunicating due to the enlarged 4 th ventricle compressing the cerebral aqueduct → ↓ CSF flow (aqueduct of Sylvius stenosis) - UWorld : Noncommunicating hydrocephalus ma

Chiari {{c2:: II }} malformation commonly results in aqueductal stenosis , which causes {{c1:: hydrocephalus }} ||| - Specifically, non-communicating hydrocephalus - Downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis & tonsils obstructs CSF flow through the foramen magnum - AKA Arnold-Chiari malformatio
Chiari {{c2::II}} malformation is often associated with lumbosacral {{c1::myelomeningocele}} ||| Causes paralysis/sensory loss at and below the level of the lesion Chiari II = mye I omeningoce I e
The brainstem is divisible into three continuous parts: the {{c1::midbrain}}, {{c2::pons}}, and {{c3::medulla}} ||| Photo credit: OpenStax , CC BY 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons
The cerebellum consists of a midline {{c1::vermis}} and two lateral {{c2:: hemispheres }} on each side ||| i.e., an intermediate and lateral hemisphere
Tonsillar herniation involves displacement of the cerebellar tonsils into the {{c1:: foramen magnum }} ||| Cerebellar tonsil herniation → brainstem compression → death

{{c1:: Non-communicating ( obstructive )}} hydrocephalus is caused by structural blockage of CSF within ventricular circulation ||| - e.g., cerebral aqueductal stenosis, colloid cyst blocking foramen of Monro, tumors, **obstruction of foramina of Luschka - vs. communicating hydrocephalus with no sig

{{c1:: Pyloric stenosis }} is a congenital hypertrophy of the pyloric smooth muscle ||| Narrowing of the pylorus
What is the most common cause of gastric outlet obstruction (GOO) in infants ? {{c1::Pyloric stenosis (1:600)}} |||

How soon after birth does pyloric stenosis typically present? {{c1::~ 2 - 6 weeks}} ||| - Takes time for hypertrophy to develop; helps distinguish from intestinal atresia (bilious vomit within 1-2 days)

Pyloric stenosis typically presents with {{c1:: nonbilious ::bilious or nonbilious}}, projectile vomiting ||| Nonbilious vomiting is an important distinguishing feature from intestinal atresia (bilious)
{{c2:: Pyloric stenosis }} often presents with a palpable "{{c1:: olive }} -like " mass in the epigastric region of the abdomen |||
Pyloric stenosis may present with visible {{c1:: peristalsis }} ||| Watch 'Peristaltic Waves in Pyloric Stenosis', - Mahmood Ahmad, via YouTube (0:19)

Intestinal atresia presents with abdominal distension and {{c1:: bilious ::bilious or nonbilious}} vomiting ||| - e.g., duodenal, jejunal, ileal atresia - Bilious vomiting is an important distinguishing feature from pyloric stenosis (nonbilious)

How soon after birth does intestinal atresia typically present? {{c1::~ 1 - 2 days}} ||| - e.g., duodenal, jejunal, ileal atresia - Helps distinguish from pyloric stenosis → non bilious vomit within 2 - 6 weeks Ileal atresia: Image(s) provided by www.radiologyassistant.nl . Used with permission.
Duodenal {{c1::atresia}} is a congenital failure of the duodenum to recanalize |||
{{c2:: Duodenal }} atresia is associated with {{c1:: Down }} syndrome ||| Results from the failure of the duodenal lumen to recanalize " D uodenal atresia = D own syndrome"
